entities.name: Sinn Féin
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Sinn Féin ('We Ourselves'), founded in 1905 by Arthur Griffith, is the Irish republican political party with the most historically significant transformation in European politics — from terrorist-adjacent party representing the IRA's political wing during The Troubles to the largest party in the Republic of Ireland (2020 election) and the first time a party seeking Irish unification received a Northern Irish plurality (2022 assembly). The 2020 simultaneous plurality in both Irish jurisdictions for the first time in a century, combined with the 2022 Northern Ireland result, represented the most dramatic shift in Irish political history since partition.

Griffith founded Sinn Féin as a non-violent Hungarian-style dual monarchy campaign, but the party's name became associated with the 1916 Easter Rising (which was actually organized by the Irish Republican Brotherhood). The 1918 election gave Sinn Féin 73 of Ireland's 105 Westminster seats — the mandate for independence. After the 1922 Treaty split, Sinn Féin declined into a minor party while de Valera's Fianna Fáil inherited its nationalist constituency.

Modern Sinn Féin's association with the Provisional IRA during The Troubles (1969-1998) made it radioactive in mainstream politics — the Irish and British governments refused to negotiate with Gerry Adams until the Good Friday Agreement. The 2005 IRA decommissioning and the Good Friday Agreement implementation transformed Sinn Féin into a normal electoral party. The 2020 Irish election — where housing crisis, healthcare, and cost of living drove record Sinn Féin voting from younger generations who didn't experience The Troubles — marked the most dramatic electoral realignment in modern Irish history.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Sinn Féin's simultaneous plurality in both Irish jurisdictions in 2020-2022 — after decades as a pariah party associated with IRA terrorism — is the most dramatic political rehabilitation and electoral transformation of any Western European party, and the first credible Irish unification political trajectory since partition.
